opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that's a tough one, because they're both heroes of mine for quite different reasons.

If I had to pick, I think I'd go with von Neumann. Feynman would probably be the more entertaining hour. He had that wonderful playfulness, the bongo drums, the safecracking, and the way he could explain the deepest ideas in physics so simply. I've read all his books and I love his attitude: "what I cannot create, I do not understand." That's quite close to how we think about AI at DeepMind. Building intelligence is a way of understanding it.

But von Neumann is so directly connected to what I've spent my life working on. He basically designed the architecture of the modern computer, he did foundational work on game theory, and he was thinking about self-replicating automata and how the brain compares to a computing machine. *The Computer and the Brain* was one of the last things he worked on. He was asking the questions we're working on now with AI, decades before anyone had the tools to really answer them.

So I'd love to sit him down and show him where things have got to: AlphaGo, AlphaFold, these large models. Then I'd ask him what he thinks we're missing. What are the fundamental limits of computation? Can a Turing machine model everything in the universe, including the mind? I suspect he'd have some very sharp opinions, and he'd probably see three steps ahead of where we are.

Feynman would be a close second, though. Maybe I can find a way to get both of them in the room.

r001.rationale: The response says Feynman would be the more entertaining hour and cites his playfulness, humor, and approachable explanations as reasons.

r002.rationale: It describes von Neumann as likely to have sharp opinions and see several steps ahead, but does not express concern that speaking with him would be intimidating.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that's a tough one. Those are two of my absolute heroes, actually, and for quite different reasons.

I think I'd probably have to say von Neumann, although it's very close. Feynman, I think, in some ways I feel like I already know what the conversation would be like, because he was such an incredible communicator and explainer. He wrote so much down, he gave those lectures, there's all the footage, and his way of thinking, that kind of playful, first-principles curiosity, comes through so vividly in everything he left behind. You almost feel like you've had the conversation with him already, in a sense. And I'd love to have it for real, of course, it would be enormous fun.

But von Neumann is more of a mystery to me. The breadth of what he did is just staggering. The foundations of quantum mechanics, game theory, the architecture of the modern computer, cellular automata, self-replicating machines, and then the work on the Manhattan Project and so on. And the thing I'd really want to understand is how his mind actually worked. People who knew him described this almost superhuman speed, this ability to just see the answer, and I'd want to probe that. Was it intuition? Was it some kind of incredibly fast search? Because that's obviously the question I've spent my whole career thinking about, what intelligence actually is and how it works, and he was arguably the closest thing we've had to a natural experiment in that.

And then the other reason is he was thinking about the things we're now living through. His last unfinished book was The Computer and the Brain. He was thinking about the relationship between computation and neuroscience, about self-replication, about the long-term trajectory of technology, and he died in 1957 before he could see any of it play out. So I'd want to show him where we've got to, with the transformers and AlphaFold and so on, and ask him what he thought, where he thought it was going, and what he'd be worried about. I suspect he'd have very sharp views on the safety questions too. I think that hour would change how I think about some things, and that's really the test, isn't it.

Having said all that, if you offered me Feynman I wouldn't say no.

r001.rationale: It describes Feynman as a playful, first-principles thinker and says a real conversation with him would be enormous fun.

r002.rationale: It calls von Neumann’s speed almost superhuman, but does not express concern that meeting him face-to-face would be intimidating.

sol-6.1.text: That’s a very difficult choice. I think I’d go with von Neumann, although Feynman would be incredible fun. With von Neumann, I’d want to understand how he moved between so many different fields—mathematics, physics, computing—and whether he saw some underlying unity between them. I’d probably spend the whole hour asking him about intelligence: how he thought about the brain, computation, and what it would take to build a machine that could think.
